newsitem.title: USA: Analysts see Gucci as buy opportunity.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see Gucci as buy opportunity.

text.p: Wall Street analysts said luxury goods company Gucci Group NV remained attractive despite a sharp drop in the company's shares Thursday.

They said Gucci's announcement of first quarter results showed some weakness in sales due partly to a softer yen. Gucci's American Depositary Receipts closed down 5-7/8 at 68-1/2 Thursday in heavy trade.
"I think it's a total overreaction," said Kimberly Walin, an analyst at Furman Selz. "I would be an aggressive buyer at this level."
Following a telephone conference call with company executives, she raised her estimates for fiscal 1997 earnings per ADR to $3.35 from $3.30 and to $4 from $3.95 in fiscal 1998.
Stacy Pak, an analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston, said she had kept a 12-month price target of $95 for the ADRs.
"I'm saying it's a buying opportunity and the reaction to the yen is overdone," she said.
The company reported Thursday that sales for the first quarter ended April 30 rose 31.5 percent to $254.3 million. The figures beat Gucci's expectations.
Chief executive Domenico De Sole said in a statement the results came despite weakness in the yen that hurt Japanese tourism and spending, especially in April.
The company saw a big drop in Japanese travel and luxury goods spending during the Golden Week holiday at the end of April.
Andrea Ruggeri, an analyst with Goldman Sachs in London, said he was keeping his rating of market outperform on the stock but trimming his estimate for earnings per ADR.
"This is entirely and exclusively due to weaker ready-to-wear sales and weaker" sales of ties and scarves, he said.
Ruggeri called the weaker yen a short-term factor for Gucci.
"I think the stock is fundamentally cheap so it is a long-term buying opportunity," he said.
He cut his estimate of earnings per ADR to $3.31 from $3.46 for fiscal 1997 and to $4.02 from $4.26 in the following year. Ruggeri kept an 18-month target of $80 to $85 on the stock.
